learning_objective: Apply the standard right-of-way rule for converging aircraft at the same level.
question_text: Two aeroplanes of the same category are converging at approximately the same altitude. Which pilot has the right of way?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The pilot of the aeroplane on the right

choices.label: B
choices.text: The pilot of the aeroplane on the left

choices.label: C
choices.text: The pilot of the faster aeroplane

choices.label: D
choices.text: The pilot of the higher aeroplane

explanation: When two aircraft of the same category are converging at approximately the same level, the aircraft that has the other on its right must give way. Put another way, the pilot who sees the other aircraft on their right has the right of way and must maintain course/speed; the other pilot must give way, normally by turning right and not crossing ahead.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: The rule gives way to the aircraft on the right, not the left — this choice reverses the standard rule.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Relative speed does not determine right of way for converging traffic.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Relative altitude is not the deciding factor for converging traffic at approximately the same level; a separate rule (based on category, e.g. balloon over glider over airship over powered aircraft) applies when the converging aircraft are of different categories.

regulation_reference: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 923/2012 (SERA), Subpart D, Section 3, right-of-way rules for converging aircraft — exact SERA.32xx paragraph number not independently re-verified this session; mirrors ICAO Annex 2 §3.2.

subject: Air Law

learning_objective: Apply the standard right-of-way rule for two aircraft approaching head-on.
question_text: Two aeroplanes are approaching head-on, or approximately so, and there is a danger of collision. What action should each pilot take?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Each pilot alters course to the right

choices.label: B
choices.text: Each pilot alters course to the left

choices.label: C
choices.text: The pilot on the right maintains course, the other gives way

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both pilots climb to increase separation

explanation: When two aircraft are approaching head-on (or nearly so) with risk of collision, each must alter its heading to the right, so that both aircraft pass on each other's left, similar to the convention for ships and road traffic in many countries.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Turning left would keep both aircraft converging on the same side and increase, not reduce, collision risk.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: The head-on case has no 'aircraft on the right' — this is a distinct rule from the converging-traffic rule; both pilots must act.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: There is no standard rule requiring a climb in a head-on encounter; the mandated action is a turn to the right.

regulation_reference: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 923/2012 (SERA), right-of-way — approaching head-on provision; exact paragraph number not independently re-verified this session; mirrors ICAO Annex 2 §3.2.

subject: Air Law

learning_objective: Apply the standard right-of-way rule for an overtaking aircraft.
question_text: An aeroplane is overtaking another aeroplane in flight. Which statement is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The overtaking aeroplane must alter course to the right and the overtaken aeroplane has right of way

choices.label: B
choices.text: The overtaken aeroplane must descend to let the faster aeroplane pass

choices.label: C
choices.text: The overtaking aeroplane may pass on either side without altering course

choices.label: D
choices.text: The overtaken aeroplane must alter course to the left

explanation: An aircraft that is being overtaken has the right of way. The overtaking aircraft must keep out of the way of the other aircraft by altering its own course to the right, and must not cease to keep out of the way until it is entirely past and clear.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: There is no requirement for the overtaken aircraft to descend; the overtaking aircraft is the one required to manoeuvre, by turning right.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: The overtaking rule specifically mandates a right turn, not an unrestricted choice of side.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: It is the overtaking aircraft, not the overtaken aircraft, that must alter course, and the required direction is right, not left.

regulation_reference: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 923/2012 (SERA), right-of-way — overtaking provision; exact paragraph number not independently re-verified this session; mirrors ICAO Annex 2 §3.2.

learning_objective: State the right-of-way hierarchy between different categories of aircraft.
question_text: A powered aeroplane and a free balloon are converging and a risk of collision exists. Which aircraft has the right of way?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The free balloon

choices.label: B
choices.text: The powered aeroplane

choices.label: C
choices.text: Whichever aircraft is higher

choices.label: D
choices.text: Whichever aircraft is on the right

explanation: The general right-of-way hierarchy between different categories of aircraft (from highest to lowest priority) is: balloons, then gliders, then airships, then aircraft towing other aircraft or objects, then powered heavier-than-air aircraft. A free balloon therefore has right of way over a powered aeroplane, which must give way.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Powered aeroplanes rank lowest in the category hierarchy and must give way to balloons, gliders and airships.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Relative altitude is not the deciding factor when the converging aircraft are of different categories — the category hierarchy applies instead.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: The 'aircraft on the right has right of way' rule applies to aircraft of the same category converging at the same level, not to encounters between different categories.

regulation_reference: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 923/2012 (SERA), right-of-way hierarchy by category of aircraft; exact paragraph number not independently re-verified this session; mirrors ICAO Annex 2 §3.2.

learning_objective: Describe the basic characteristics of ICAO Annex 11 airspace classification, Class A.
question_text: What is a defining characteristic of Class A airspace under the ICAO airspace classification system?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Only IFR flights are permitted, and all flights are subject to air traffic control

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only VFR flights are permitted, with no ATC service

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both IFR and VFR flights are permitted with no separation service provided

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only VFR flights are permitted, subject to an ATC clearance

explanation: Class A is the most restrictive controlled airspace class in the ICAO classification: only IFR flights are permitted, all flights receive an air traffic control service, and all flights are separated from each other by ATC.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: VFR flights are not permitted at all in Class A airspace.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Class A is controlled airspace with ATC separation between all flights, and VFR flights are excluded entirely — this describes an uncontrolled class instead.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: VFR flight is prohibited in Class A regardless of clearance; only IFR flights may operate there.

regulation_reference: ICAO Annex 11, Appendix 4 airspace classification table, as implemented in the EU via Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 923/2012 (SERA), Appendix 4; exact SERA article number not independently re-verified this session.

learning_objective: State the regulatory definition of 'night' used for licensing and flight-rules purposes.
question_text: For the purposes of EASA flight crew licensing, how is 'night' generally defined?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The period between the end of evening civil twilight and the beginning of morning civil twilight

choices.label: B
choices.text: The period between sunset and sunrise only, with no twilight allowance

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any time the sun is more than 6 degrees below the horizon, regardless of twilight phase

choices.label: D
choices.text: A fixed period from 22:00 to 06:00 local time

explanation: 'Night' is generally defined as the period between the end of evening civil twilight and the beginning of morning civil twilight (or such other period as may be prescribed by the competent authority), civil twilight ending/beginning when the centre of the sun's disc is a specified number of degrees below the horizon. This extends the definition of night slightly beyond simple sunset-to-sunrise.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Using sunset/sunrise alone omits the civil twilight margin that the regulatory definition includes.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: This describes a different twilight concept (closer to nautical twilight) rather than the civil-twilight-based definition actually used.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Night is defined astronomically relative to twilight, not by a fixed clock time, since sunset/sunrise varies by date and location.

regulation_reference: Regulation (EU) No 1178/2011, Part-FCL, Annex I, Definitions — definition of 'night'; exact definitions-list numbering not independently re-verified this session.

subject: Air Law
syllabus_version: Part-FCL.215 theoretical knowledge subject 010 (Air Law) — LO numbering not independently verified this session
learning_objective: Apply the semi-circular VFR cruising-level rule above the transition altitude/3000 ft AMSL.
question_text: An aeroplane is flying VFR in cruising flight above 3000 ft AMSL on a magnetic track of 090°. Which type of cruising level must it use under the semi-circular rule?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An odd flight level or altitude plus 500 ft (e.g. FL035, FL055)

choices.label: B
choices.text: An even flight level or altitude plus 500 ft (e.g. FL045, FL065)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any flight level, since the semi-circular rule only applies to IFR flights

choices.label: D
choices.text: An odd flight level with no 500 ft addition (e.g. FL030, FL050)

explanation: Under the semi-circular cruising-level rule, VFR flights on a magnetic track from 000° to 179° use 'odd thousands plus 500 ft' (e.g. 3500 ft, 5500 ft / FL035, FL055); tracks from 180° to 359° use 'even thousands plus 500 ft'. A track of 090° falls in the 000–179° sector, so an odd-thousands-plus-500 ft level applies.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Even-thousands-plus-500 ft levels apply to tracks of 180°–359°, not to a track of 090°.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: The semi-circular rule with the +500 ft VFR offset applies to VFR cruising flight specifically (IFR flights use the same odd/even split without the +500 ft offset); it is not restricted to IFR only.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: The plain odd-thousands levels (without +500 ft) are the IFR cruising levels; VFR flights add 500 ft to those levels.

regulation_reference: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 923/2012 (SERA), cruising levels (semi-circular rule); exact SERA.5005 sub-paragraph not independently re-verified this session.
calculation_steps: Track 090° falls within the 000°–179° sector → apply 'odd thousands + 500 ft' cruising levels.
